title: EDUCATION: Everyone in Edtech Should Show Their Cards
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer responds to LA USD's draft plan limiting classroom screen time (grades 4-5 to 30 min/day, grades 2-3 to 20, grade 1 and below to zero) by challenging edtech executives who argue the debate should shift from screen time to screen value. Meyer acknowledges that honest scrutiny of most edtech products would reveal screens that pacify rather than challenge, isolate rather than connect, and reduce teacher visibility into student learning. Using Amplify Desmos Math as a concrete example, he shows what accountable edtech use looks like: students working on devices together, for just 13 total minutes across a full class period, with technology making student thinking visible to a teacher who drives whole-class conversation. Meyer calls on every edtech company to post one stationary video of a full classroom session, arguing such transparency would do more to restore or erode parent trust than any company-funded research or LinkedIn post.
points: LA USD's screen time limits: grades 4-5 capped at 30 min/day; grade 2-3 at 20; grade 1 and below at zero -- an industry-wide forcing function.
Many edtech products, under honest scrutiny, would show pacifying screens, reduced teacher visibility, and isolated rather than collaborative student work.
Good edtech: technology as a loom weaving people and ideas together, not a delivery vehicle for content to individuals.
Amplify Desmos lesson model: 13 total minutes of screen time, making student thinking visible for teacher-led discussion.
Challenge to the industry: post one unedited stationary video of a full classroom session and let parents judge.
quotes: Every edtech executive with more than 1,000 followers on LinkedIn has published their #NotAllEdtech post arguing that we should focus less on screen time and more on screen value.

To observe how many products are used in classrooms would only validate the fears of many parents -- screens that pacify rather than challenge; screens that isolate rather than connect; screens that decrease rather than increase a teacher's visibility into a student's learning.
I'd like each of my colleagues to show their cards. I'd like to see from everyone engaged in this discourse: one (1) stationary video of a full classroom session.
We use technology as a loom and weave together people and their ideas.
Parents value the human relationships that schools produce, relationships that support student learning and human flourishing. Everyone in edtech should show their cards.
